title: Two simultaneous mycetomas caused by Fusarium verticillioides and Madurella mycetomatis
case_text:
A 63 year-old man, from Azoyu, Guerrero (542 km Southeast from Mexico City), came to our service presenting 10-year nodular lesions with swelling, draining sinuses and crusting in the lower limbs, mainly distributed on the left foot and the right leg. The early lesion was a solitary nodule on the left foot, followed by the appearance of several draining nodules, close to each other. Two years after the first lesion (8 years of evolution), he developed a nodule in his right ankle, extending to the right aspect of the leg. The patient reported some pruritus and pain on palpation of both dermatoses (Figure 1) There was a history of multiple trauma on both feet, without specifying which objects caused the lesions. Mycological studies: direct examination (KOH 10%) of the discharge revealed black grains in the left foot sample and white grains on the opposite side of the same foot. On culture, both causative agents, Madurella mycetomatis and Fusarium verticillioides (formerly F. moniliforme), were eumycetes. (Figures 2 and 3). Histopathological examination of the left foot biopsy showed grains, thick hyphae, brownish pigment inside; moreover, in the right foot biopsy, plentiful granules, with a pale whitish coloration, presenting eosinophilic appearance in some areas, were reported (Figures 4 and 5). The center of these collections contained colonies of eumycetes. X-ray of the feet reported osteolysis and periostitis. After screening for renal function tests, routine blood count, G-6-PD activity and audiometry, we decided to start itraconazole 400 mg/day for 58 days and then to add dapsone (DDS) 100 mg/day. The patient did not attend the follow-up visits.
The identification of the fungi was made by traditional methods. As for M. mycetomatis, the following was observed: development of filamentous colony, folded, of brown color, with diffusible ocher pigment. Optimal temperature of growth 37  C, assimilation of lactose and negative for sucrose. Microscopically with sterile, melanized mycelium, and formation of scarce sclerotia. F. verticilloides, development of white filamentous colony, fast growing, with diffusible purple pigment. The microscopy showed short conidiophores, with abundant oval microconidia in chains and thin (3-5 septa) and straight macroconidia.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Mycetoma
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: simultaneous eumycetomas caused by Madurella mycetomatis and Fusarium verticillioides
